text: This is a loss surface seen from above, like a hiking map.
Each ring joins points of equal loss, and inner rings are lower.
The lowest point, where the loss is zero, sits right here.
The loss at any point is x squared plus four y squared.
caption: The loss at any point is x squared plus 4 y squared

text: We start out on the slope, where the loss is twenty.
caption: We start out on the slope, where the loss is 20

text: The gradient is an arrow pointing in the steepest uphill direction.
It always crosses the ring through our point at a right angle.
We want to go down, so turn the arrow right around.
The learning rate, zero point one, shrinks it to one small step.
caption: The learning rate, 0.1, shrinks it to one small step

text: Take that step, and the loss falls from twenty to ten point four.
caption: Take that step, and the loss falls from 20 to 10.4

text: The slope is different here, so measure the gradient again and step.
Measure, step downhill, and the loss drops to about four point two.
caption: Measure, step downhill, and the loss drops to about 4.2

text: Each step is shorter, because the slope flattens as we descend.
After five steps the loss is about one point seven, still creeping along.
caption: After 5 steps the loss is about 1.7, still creeping along

text: That is the whole rule: subtract learning rate times gradient, then repeat.
Now go back to the start and double the learning rate.
The first step is twice as long and crosses the valley floor.
The next step crosses straight back, so the path starts to zigzag.
Each bounce is smaller, and the loss is already below one.
caption: Each bounce is smaller, and the loss is already below 1

text: Four zigzag steps reach a lower loss than five careful ones did.
caption: 4 zigzag steps reach a lower loss than 5 careful ones did

text: Now push further, with a learning rate of zero point three.
caption: Now push further, with a learning rate of 0.3

text: This step leaps clean across the valley and up the far wall.
The loss looked fine at ten point four, but now it rises.
caption: The loss looked fine at 10.4, but now it rises

text: Steeper walls mean bigger gradients, so every leap is longer than the last.
The loss has climbed past thirty: this run is diverging.
caption: The loss has climbed past 30: this run is diverging

text: Same map, same start: only the learning rate was changed.
Too small a rate is safe, but the descent is slow.
Too large, and every step overshoots the valley and climbs.
Follow the slope downhill, and choose your step size with care.
